newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somaliland president re-elected in landslide vote.
newsitem.headline: Somaliland president re-elected in landslide vote.

text.p: Mohamed Ibrahim Egal was carried shoulder-high by jubilant supporters when he was on Sunday re-elected president of the Somaliland Republic, which has not been internationally recognised since breaking away from the rest of Somalia in 1991.
Egal scored a landslide victory, gaining 223 votes in the 315-member National Communities Conference which acted as an electoral college.
Somaliland's president since 1993 - two years after it declared itself an independent republic - Egal was re-elected for a five-year term.

His country covers the area of the former British Somaliland Protectorate, which joined with neighbouring Italian Somalia to form the independent Republic of Somalia in 1960. It declared itself independent in 1991, after the ousting of dictator Mohamed Siad Barre and the collapse of effective government in Somalia.
Somaliland has an estimated population of one million and the capital, Hargeisa, has some 80,000 residents.

The conference had been sitting for 131 days, debating new constitutional proposals for Somaliland. Originally, 10 candidates put themselves forward, but on Sunday only two, Egal and former finance and foreign minister Suleiman Mohamed Aden, remained effectively in the running. Aden got 90 votes while former Mayor of Hargeisa Mohamed Hashi Elmi got two.
After the result was announced, Aden congratulated Egal on winning in a fair and open election. He called on Egal to respect human and minority rights.
Egal said: "I am president for all the people of Somaliland -- let us forget the heat of the campaign and work together for the good of the nation."
Egal, 67, was prime minister of the Somali Republic before being jailed for 12 years by Siad Barre when he took power in a coup in 1969.
Egal is loud in his criticism of the international community for its refusal to recognise Somaliland's declaration of independence.
Sunday's election is due to be the last with an electoral college as direct elections are proposed in the new constitution, already approved by the Hargeisa conference.

The presidential election comes at a time when government and opposition forces have reached agreement to end a long period of conflict, with armed opposition groups being merged in the country's armed forces.
The new political climate has sparked a mass return of refugees who fled into neighbouring Ethiopia after the collapse of Somalia in 1991.
Jubilant crowds have been welcoming convoys of returning refugees at the border before they continued their journey to their former home areas.
Somaliland has rejected proposals to end its break with the rest of Somalia -- a decision reiterated after a recent unity conference by Somali factions held in Ethiopia.
